title: The Pulsing Moss Mystery
markdown:
The sun blasted through Asha's window. Today was field-guide day. She bounced out of bed buzzing.

"Drift! Ready!"

Drift, her seal pal, popped up with a happy bark. Their collecting kits waited by the door.

They dashed into the crisp morning. Birds burst into song. The Whispering Woods smelled of damp soil, and sunlight dappled the path. Asha skidded.

"Whoa. Drift. Look."

Beneath gnarled roots, something pulsed with a faint greenish light. Delicate tendrils twitched. Drift nudged it — boop — and tiny specks drifted out.

"It's releasing something." Asha peered through her magnifying glass. Dark spots on the mossy cushion swelled and dimmed. It was not quite a plant she knew, and not quite an animal. "This doesn't fit the pages."

Drift nosed a fallen leaf across it. Shadow fell. The pulsing slowed; the light dulled. Then plump dewdrops landed from the roots above. The cushion brightened and pulsed again, and more specks lifted, like pale dust that wanted to travel.

Asha's mind raced. Gran Mae's voice lived in her pocket: Observe the conditions. Life adapts.

She had been taught that green things drink light. This one had dimmed in shade and woken when it was wet. "The specks are a bit like seeds," she whispered, "but they don't wait for a flower. They leave when it's damp."

She lifted a small piece into her kit and added a drop of water, copying the dew. She kept it out of the harsh sun, the way the roots had. Tiny buds swelled on the damp, shaded sample.

"It needs moisture, and it doesn't like frying in the open," she told Drift. "The dark under the roots keeps it from drying. That's not the same as needing night."

Drift barked, which Asha took for peer review.

Back at Gran Mae's cottage, warm smells met them. Gran Mae's eyes twinkled.

"What have we here?"

Asha explained the pulse, the specks, the leaf, the dew. Gran Mae examined the sample under her stronger glass.

"Remarkable. Not a misfit, my girl. A partnership. This is lichen — a fungus and a tiny alga living together. The fungus makes the cushion and holds water. The alga, tucked inside, uses what light it can get to make food. Damp shade suits them. When the cushion is wet enough, it lets go those specks — little starter-packs, fungus and alga together — so they can start again on the next root."

She pointed. "See? Green cells catching light. Fungal threads holding on and sipping the damp. Two lives, one address."

Asha beamed. "So we don't force it into plant or animal. We classify it by how it lives and how it makes more of itself."

"Exactly. Classification is a way of noticing kinship, not a box for shoving leftovers." Gran Mae's mouth tilted, dry as good toast. "A fantastic find. We'll give it a page that tells the truth."

Asha's heart thumped. She could already see the drawing: roots, dew, specks, two partners.

"I wonder," she said, "whether the sunny rock by the creek has a different lichen — one that likes more light — and whether its specks travel the same way, or only when the fog comes in."

Drift sneezed a drop of kit-water, which seemed, on the whole, like agreement.
